questions.question: A service handles 600,000 predictions per second and each prediction reads 80 online features. What feature-value read rate must the online store sustain before headroom?
options: 7.5 million values per second
48 million values per second
600,000 values per second
480 million values per day
questions.explanation: Multiply prediction QPS by features per prediction: 600,000 x 80 = 48,000,000 feature values per second. Serving capacity must account for feature fan-out, not only request count.

questions.question: Why is a point-in-time join required when building a training set?
options: It lets training use the newest value available today for every historical label.
It ensures each feature value was available at or before the prediction time, preventing future-information leakage.
It guarantees all feature values are strongly consistent across regions.
It eliminates the need to retain feature versions.
questions.explanation: A point-in-time join filters feature values by the example's event time. Without it, future observations leak into training and make offline evaluation unrealistically optimistic.

questions.question: A candidate transform is correct, but its online materialization is 85 seconds behind a 60-second freshness SLA. What should the release process do?
options: Promote the candidate because the transform logic is correct.
Serve the late values because a successful lookup is always better than a fallback.
Pin the last compatible model and feature bundle until the candidate meets its freshness contract.
Rebuild every historical training set before making a serving decision.
questions.explanation: The candidate is not safe to promote until its online values satisfy the freshness contract. Keep the prior compatible manifest live rather than creating silent training-serving skew.

questions.question: Which item belongs in a feature bundle manifest used for production inference?
options: Only the feature names, because source and transform details are implementation concerns.
The model version, feature definition versions, freshness and fallback rules, and release approvals.
Only the online-store shard count and cache eviction policy.
The current average model accuracy across all customers.
questions.explanation: A manifest makes the release reproducible: it ties a model to the precise feature semantics, freshness boundary, fallback behavior, and approved bundle that were evaluated together.

questions.question: The online feature store misses its deadline. When is it defensible to serve a last-good or default feature bundle?
options: Whenever returning any prediction is more convenient than returning an error.
Only when the model was evaluated with that declared fallback, its age is within policy, and the fallback is recorded for reconciliation.
Only after retrying the online store indefinitely.
Never; online feature stores must always fail the entire product request.
questions.explanation: Fallback is part of the model contract, not an invisible availability trick. It needs a compatible evaluated bundle, an explicit freshness limit, and a decision record.

questions.question: Which monitoring signal most directly detects a training-serving parity regression before it becomes a model-quality incident?
options: Comparing batch and streaming transform outputs, null rates, timestamps, and versions over the same event-time interval.
Tracking only average CPU utilization of the online store.
Measuring how many feature names exist in the catalog.
Alerting only when model accuracy drops after labels arrive.
questions.explanation: Parity monitoring compares the two ways feature values are produced and served. This exposes semantic, timestamp, and missingness differences before delayed labels reveal degraded model outcomes.
